title: Hierarchical Procedural Meta-Reasoning for Generalizable Multimodal Agents
one_liner: Teach an agent to gather and use task procedures from several sources so it can act across changing apps and workflows.
lead: Agents that act on phones or desktops often fail on new tasks even when they see the screen correctly. The missing piece is usually procedural knowledge: the ordered steps needed to finish the job in a given app or across several apps. This paper builds an agent that represents those steps explicitly and decides when to rely on built-in knowledge and when to fetch extra procedures from outside sources, because strong action selection depends on having the right task procedure available at the moment of choice.

problem.h2: Why screen understanding alone does not give reliable action plans
paras: A grounded agent can read buttons, forms, and menus. That still does not tell it the exact sequence needed to finish a task across real applications. App versions change, task conventions differ, and the same goal may require different sequences depending on the current state.

The central failure is missing procedure knowledge. If the agent knows what is on the screen but not the ordered recipe for the task, it can pick locally plausible actions that derail the whole job. The paper addresses this by treating procedures as first-class inputs because acting well depends on matching the current task to a relevant step-by-step plan.

callout.html: Represent task procedures explicitly and let the agent choose among procedure sources, because generalization improves when action decisions are conditioned on the right procedure rather than on raw screen context alone.

steps.text: Store task knowledge as explicit step sequences so the agent can inspect and condition on them during action selection.
Use internal knowledge when available and fetch outside procedures when needed, because one source alone may miss app-specific detail.
Estimate which procedure best matches the current task and interface state so the grounded agent follows the most relevant guide.

steps.b: Condition each action on the chosen procedure.
steps.text: Use both the current screen and the selected procedure so local actions stay consistent with the full task sequence.

steps.b: Train across varied tasks and app settings.
steps.text: Expose the system to diverse tasks, versions, and workflows because generalization requires experience with procedural variation.

paras: The paper changes grounded action selection from screen-only control into procedure-aware control that can draw task knowledge from multiple sources.
object.object: the source of task knowledge used for action decisions

hidden.name: procedure-task match quality
paras: The key hidden quantity is how well a candidate procedure matches the actual task and app state. A procedure may be valid in general and still be poor for this case because the interface version differs or the workflow spans extra tools.

The framework estimates that match through meta-reasoning over available procedure sources. This matters because a grounded agent only benefits from explicit procedures when the chosen one covers the right steps in the right order.

cells: retrieved help useful because it matches the app
heat.caption: Darker cells mark situations where the selected procedure truly fits the current task.

reads.html: This quantity asks whether the agent has the right recipe for the job. Success rises when the recipe fits because each local click or edit is then chosen in service of the full task.
The method improves generalization because it explicitly selects and conditions on task procedures from different knowledge sources, so the grounded policy can adapt to task and interface variation.

paras: Pure fine-tuning often ties behavior too closely to seen screens and seen action traces. That leaves the agent brittle on new workflows because it lacks an explicit description of what the task requires. Procedure-aware control inserts that missing structure: the agent sees not only the current interface but also the ordered plan it should be following.

Multiple sources matter because one procedure source can be incomplete. General knowledge may cover common actions, while fetched external guidance may cover a new app version or a specialized workflow. Meta-reasoning over those sources helps because the agent can choose the most suitable procedure for the present task instead of following one default plan everywhere.

The hierarchy matters because high-level procedure choice and low-level action grounding are different decisions. The first picks the right recipe; the second executes the next step on the current screen. Separating them improves transfer because the same high-level procedure can survive screen variation while the grounded controller adapts the exact click sequence.

stages.s: gather procedures from internal and external sources
pick the next grounded action under that procedure
task completed across apps and versions

math.h2: Choose actions with a matched procedure
math.words: A simple summary is to score a candidate action by how well it advances the chosen procedure on the current screen, because the best local action is the one that moves the procedure forward.
math.equation: score(action) = screen_fit(action) + alpha * procedure_progress(action) - beta * procedure_mismatch
symbols: how appropriate the action is for the visible interface state
weight on advancing the selected procedure
how much the action completes the next intended step
penalty on following a poor or outdated procedure
how badly the current procedure fits the task and app state

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Action A clicks the visible booking button, so screen_fit = 4 and procedure_progress = 5.
Action B opens an unrelated settings page, so screen_fit = 2 and procedure_progress = 0.
If alpha = 2 and beta * procedure_mismatch = 1 for the chosen plan, Action A scores 4 + 10 - 1 = 13.
The agent prefers Action A because it moves the selected procedure forward on the current screen.

math.note: The paper's full framework includes hierarchical procedure selection, but the central objective is to prefer actions that both fit the screen and advance the right procedure.

charts.title: Grounded agents without explicit procedures
charts.note: Screen-grounded control alone struggles when tasks require ordered knowledge that is not obvious from the current view.

charts.title: Procedure-aware meta-reasoning
charts.note: The paper reports strong gains because explicit procedures let the agent carry task structure across changing interfaces.

items.b: Retrieved procedures can be wrong or stale.
items.html: If the outside guidance reflects an old interface or a different workflow, the agent may follow incorrect steps because the selected recipe no longer matches the real task.

items.b: Meta-reasoning can choose the wrong source.
items.html: If the source selector overvalues familiar procedures, the grounded controller may never use the better app-specific guide because it trusts the default too much.
If the steps are high-level only, the grounded controller may still face ambiguity at key branch points because the plan does not specify enough detail.

The method works when the system can retrieve relevant procedures and score their fit to the current task, because then each grounded action is guided by the best available recipe instead of by screen cues alone.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build an Android-style task set with several workflows such as ordering food, booking travel, and sharing results across apps. Compare a grounded screen agent with and without explicit procedures. Provide task procedures from built-in knowledge, retrieved guides, or both, and vary app versions so the procedure selector must decide which source to trust.
The demo should show that completion improves when the agent chooses the right procedure source and then grounds each step on the visible interface, because that is the paper's core mechanism.
demo.closing: A convincing demo must show transfer across changed apps and multi-app workflows, because the claimed benefit comes from carrying explicit procedure knowledge into settings that differ from the training traces.
